title: Mark at the Table
subtitle: Eight sessions through the shortest Gospel, built for a table where not everyone believes
summary: Mark is the shortest Gospel and the fastest moving. The earliest church memory, passed down from a bishop named Papias in the second century, says Mark wrote down what Peter preached, and most scholars date it within about forty years of the events it describes. It was written to force one question: who is this man. This study walks a mixed table through Mark in eight sessions, and it assumes nothing. A skeptic can sit at this table and never be cornered, because the study does not ask anyone to believe before they have read. It asks everyone to read honestly and answer for themselves.
setting: A living room, a kitchen table, a back booth. Believers, skeptics, and the undecided sit as equals. One Gospel, read out loud.
forWho: Anyone curious about Jesus, and especially the person who does not believe and is tired of being sold to. Bring a friend who thinks church people never listen.
rhythm: Eight sessions, about an hour each. Weekly works. So does every other week. The pace matters less than the honesty.
leaderNote: Do not assume belief, ever. When you write the questions in your head, write them for the most skeptical person at the table, because if the table is safe for that person it is safe for everyone. Your job is to keep the text open and protect the honest question, not to win. If someone senses a trap, the table is over, and they will be right to leave. Say I do not know when you do not know, and go find out together. Mark does not flinch from the hard question and neither should you. Trust the text to do its own work.

sessions.title: The Announcement
sessions.bigIdea: Mark opens with a claim, not a suggestion. Before anyone decides what to do with Jesus, they should at least know what is actually being claimed about him.
sessions.open: What did you grow up assuming Jesus was? A teacher, a myth, a moral example, a savior, a stranger? Where did that picture come from?
sessions.read: Read Mark 1:1-15 out loud. The first line calls itself the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Gospel meant an announcement of news, the word a herald used for a victory or a new king, not a word for advice. Then Jesus arrives announcing that the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent and believe in the gospel.
observe: What titles and claims are stacked up in the first verse alone, before any story is told?
Jesus announces something has happened and calls for a response. What are the two verbs he uses in verse 15?
talk: An announcement is different from advice. Advice says do this and life improves. News says this happened, now respond. Whether or not you believe it, what changes if Christianity is claiming to be news rather than advice?
Mark gives no birth story and no childhood. He starts at a sprint. Why might a writer in a hurry think this announcement could not wait?
What would you need to see in the next seven sessions to take this claim seriously? Say it plainly. The table can handle it.
sessions.practice: Read Mark chapters 1 through 3 on your own this week, fifteen minutes total. Mark one moment that surprised you and one that bothered you. Bring both back to the table.
sessions.send: You do not have to believe the announcement tonight. You have to know what it says. Now you do.
sessions.passItOn: Think of one person who would enjoy arguing about this around a table. Invite them to the next session. A mixed table is a better table.

sessions.title: The Authority Problem
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus does something only God has the right to do, in a crowded room, and then backs the claim with something visible. Mark wants you to feel the scandal, not skip it.
sessions.open: Who has the right to forgive a wrong done to you? Could a stranger off the street forgive it on your behalf? Why not?
sessions.read: Read Mark 2:1-12. Four men tear open a roof to lower a paralyzed friend to Jesus, and Jesus says something nobody expected: son, your sins are forgiven. The scribes in the room are appalled, and their logic is sound. Who can forgive sins but God alone? Jesus does not soften the claim. He says the healing happens so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.
observe: The scribes never say their objection out loud, yet Jesus answers it. What exactly is their objection, and is it a reasonable one?
Jesus links an invisible claim, forgiveness, to a visible test, the man walking. Why offer a test at all?
talk: The scribes are often played as villains, but their theology is correct. Only the offended party can forgive, and every sin offends God. If Jesus is not God, what is the most honest thing to call this scene?
Notice the friends. The paralyzed man never says a word, and Mark says Jesus saw their faith. What does it suggest that other people carried him there?
If someone told you your sins were forgiven, would that land as good news, as presumption, or as nothing at all? Be honest about which, and why.
sessions.practice: This week, notice one moment when you wanted forgiveness or needed to give it, at work, at home, in traffic. Write one sentence about what forgiveness actually cost in that moment.
sessions.send: The claim on the table is not that Jesus was kind. It is that he had authority. Kindness asks nothing of you. Authority does.
sessions.passItOn: Retell this roof story to one person this week in your own words, no commentary added. It is a story people want to finish hearing.

sessions.title: A Strange Kingdom
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus describes his kingdom in riddles about seed and soil, and the picture is nothing like power as anyone practices it. Small, slow, buried, and then suddenly everywhere.
sessions.open: Tell the table about something small in your life that turned out to matter far more than its size, a habit, a sentence someone said, a chance meeting.
sessions.read: Read Mark 4:1-9, the parable of the sower, and then Mark 4:26-34. A farmer scatters seed and sleeps, and the ground produces by itself, he knows not how. The kingdom of God is like a grain of mustard seed, the smallest of the seeds, which grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.
observe: In the parable of the sower, the same seed lands on four kinds of ground. What actually varies, the seed or the soil?
In the parables of growth, what does the farmer control and what does he plainly not control?
talk: Empires announce themselves with armies and monuments. Jesus compares his kingdom to a seed you could lose in your pocket. If you were inventing a religion to impress people, would you write it this way? What do you make of the choice?
Which soil is the most honest description of you right now, the path, the rocks, the thorns, or the good ground? No one at this table is grading you.
The farmer sleeps and rises and the seed grows, he knows not how. Where does that picture comfort you, and where does it frustrate the part of you that wants control?
sessions.practice: Plant one small thing this week and do not force it. Read a chapter of Mark, ask one honest question of someone you trust, or sit in silence for five minutes. Let it be seed, not performance.
sessions.send: Nothing about this kingdom is loud. That is either its weakness or its genius. Keep reading before you decide.
sessions.passItOn: Ask one person this week what they think makes a life grow. Just listen. You are learning the soil around you.

sessions.title: The Question Itself
sessions.bigIdea: Halfway through his book, Mark stops the action and puts one question in the road: who do you say that I am. Every reader has to walk past it, and there is no neutral route around.
sessions.open: What is the most common opinion about Jesus among the people you know? A good teacher, a legend, a prophet, something else?
sessions.read: Read Mark 8:27-38. Jesus asks his friends what the crowds are saying, and the answers are flattering. John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. Then he turns the question on them. But who do you say that I am? Peter answers, you are the Christ. Immediately Jesus begins teaching that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, and be killed, and Peter rebukes him for it. Then Jesus says that whoever would come after him must deny himself and take up his cross and follow. For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?
observe: The crowd's answers all make Jesus a great man. What is the difference between every one of them and Peter's answer?
The moment Peter gets the title right, he gets the mission wrong. What does Peter object to, and how hard does Jesus push back?
talk: A good teacher is easy to admire and easy to ignore. The Christ can be neither. Which category costs you less, and is that part of its appeal?
Peter wanted a Christ without a cross, a winner without the suffering. Where do people, religious and not, still want exactly that?
Answer the question at the table tonight, in a sentence, at whatever honesty you can afford. Who do you say he is? An I do not know yet is a real answer here.
sessions.practice: Write your one sentence answer somewhere you will see it this week. Do not polish it. At the end of the week, read it again and note whether anything in you pushed back.
sessions.send: The crowds had opinions. The disciples got asked the question. Tonight you stopped being a crowd.
sessions.passItOn: Ask one friend this week, with no follow-up speech, who do you think Jesus actually was? Then do the hard part. Say nothing and listen.

sessions.title: The Servant King
sessions.bigIdea: Two disciples ask for thrones and Jesus gives them a definition instead. Greatness in his kingdom is service, and he sets himself as the pattern, a king who came to die.
sessions.open: Describe the best boss, coach, or leader you have ever had. What made them different from the worst one?
sessions.read: Read Mark 10:35-45. James and John ask for the seats of honor, and the other ten are furious, likely because they wanted the same seats. Jesus gathers them and turns the whole structure over. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
observe: What exactly do James and John ask for, and what does their timing tell you, coming right after Jesus has again predicted his death?
In verse 45, Jesus states his own mission in one sentence. What are its two halves?
talk: Every institution you have ever been part of, including churches, runs on rank somewhere. What would it actually cost an organization to run on service instead? Be specific about the cost.
Ransom is a debt word. It says someone is held and a price buys them out. Whatever you believe, what is Jesus claiming his death will accomplish, and for whom?
The critique of power hungry religion is fair, and this passage agrees with it. Does it surprise you that the sharpest critique of religious ambition sits inside the Gospel itself?
sessions.practice: Do one act of service this week that nobody will see and you cannot be credited for. Notice how much you want to mention it. That noticing is the lesson.
sessions.send: The kingdoms you know climb. This one kneels. Hold that picture. The next two sessions test whether he meant it.
sessions.passItOn: Serve someone this week who could never repay you or advance you. Quiet service is the argument no one can rebut.

sessions.title: The Confrontation
sessions.bigIdea: In his last week Jesus walks into the temple and the trap questions start. He confronts corrupt religion to its face and refuses to be owned by any political side. Both facts still sting.
sessions.open: When has an institution you trusted, religious or otherwise, used its power to protect itself instead of the people it served? What did that do to your trust?
sessions.read: Read Mark 11:15-18. Jesus drives the merchants out of the temple courts, quoting the prophets: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations, but you have made it a den of robbers. The chief priests start planning to destroy him that same day. Then read Mark 12:13-17, where Pharisees and Herodians, enemies of each other, team up with a trap question about taxes. Jesus answers, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's, and Mark says they marveled at him.
observe: The court Jesus clears was the one place Gentiles, the outsiders, were allowed to pray. Who is actually being robbed in his quotation, money aside?
The tax question is built so that either answer destroys him, rebel or collaborator. How does his answer refuse both boxes?
talk: Many people leave faith because of corrupt religion. Jesus' angriest recorded moment is aimed at corrupt religion. What do you do with the fact that he is on that side of the complaint?
Caesar's image was on the coin. Genesis says God's image is on the human being. Follow the logic of Jesus' answer: what belongs to Caesar, and what does he say belongs to God?
Every political movement since has tried to recruit Jesus. Based on these two scenes, would he be safe for any party to invite on stage? What does that tell you?
sessions.practice: Notice one moment this week when you are tempted to use faith, or your rejection of faith, as a badge for your political team. Just notice it, and name it at the next table.
sessions.send: He would not be bought by the temple or by Caesar. Whatever he is, he is not anyone's mascot.
sessions.passItOn: When a friend says the church is full of hypocrites this week, try agreeing, and then tell them about the man who flipped the tables. Watch what that honesty opens.

sessions.title: The Cross
sessions.bigIdea: Mark slows down for the death of Jesus and hides nothing, the mockery, the darkness, the cry of abandonment. The first human to call him the Son of God after his death is the Roman soldier who watched him die.
sessions.open: Why do you think an execution device became the most recognized symbol in the world? What does it take for a symbol of shame to turn into that?
sessions.read: Read Mark 15:22-39, slowly, and let it be as heavy as it is. Jesus is crucified between two robbers while the crowd mocks him with his own words. Darkness covers the land for three hours. Then Jesus cries out, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? He utters a loud cry and breathes his last, the temple curtain tears from top to bottom, and the centurion who stood facing him says, truly this man was the Son of God.
observe: Count the voices that mock him and notice what they demand: save yourself, come down, and we will believe. What kind of proof are they asking for?
His final words in Mark are a question of abandonment, taken from the opening of Psalm 22. Who is the one person in the scene who concludes he is the Son of God, and what had that man watched?
talk: The mockers offer a deal, come down and we will believe. He stays. If the ransom saying from session five was true, why could he not take the deal? Follow the story's own logic, whether or not you share it.
Christianity puts a cry of godforsakenness at the center of its story about God. For anyone who has felt abandoned by God, what is the difference between a God who never suffered and this one?
The centurion was a professional at executions and a pagan. Something in how this man died convinced him. What do you make of Mark handing the verdict to an outsider?
sessions.practice: Read Psalm 22 once this week, the psalm Jesus quoted from the cross, and note where it ends up by its final verses. Bring one observation back to the table.
sessions.send: They said come down and we will believe. He stayed up, and a Roman believed. Sit with that this week. Do not rush it.
sessions.passItOn: Someone you know is carrying a grief they think God is nowhere near. You now know a God who cried the same cry. You do not need answers to sit with them this week. Go sit.

sessions.title: The Unfinished Ending
sessions.bigIdea: The oldest manuscripts of Mark end mid-scene, with an empty tomb, a promise, and women fleeing in fear. The story refuses to close because the reader is meant to finish it.
sessions.open: Have you ever had news so large you could not speak at first? What did the silence before the telling feel like?
sessions.read: Read Mark 16:1-8. The women come at sunrise to anoint a body and find the stone rolled away and a young man in white saying, he has risen, he is not here, and sending them to tell the disciples and Peter that Jesus is going before them to Galilee. Verse 8 says they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. Be honest with the table about the manuscripts: the two oldest complete copies of Mark end right there, at verse 8, and most modern Bibles mark the longer ending as a later addition. Mark, as far as we can tell, chose to stop mid-breath.
observe: The messenger names Peter specifically, the man whose last act in this Gospel was denying Jesus three times. Why single him out?
The tomb is empty and the witnesses are terrified women whose testimony counted for little in that culture. If the story were invented to persuade, what would you have written differently?
talk: Every explanation of Easter morning has to account for something: the empty tomb, the transformed disciples who died for the claim, the church that exploded out of the city where anyone could check the grave. Which explanation seems most plausible to you tonight, and what is the strongest point against your own view?
Mark ends with fear and silence, not triumph, and yet you are reading his book two thousand years later, which means somebody eventually spoke. What do you think broke the silence?
You have now read a whole Gospel. Go back to session four's question one last time: who do you say that he is? Has your answer moved, even an inch, and in which direction?
sessions.practice: Write down where you honestly stand after eight sessions, believing, doubting, undecided, unsettled, and one question you still carry. Share it with one person from this table over coffee this week.
sessions.send: Mark left the ending open on purpose. The women ran from the tomb into the rest of the story. So do you.
sessions.passItOn: This study only exists because someone finally told someone. If these eight weeks were worth your time, you can lead them for another table exactly as they were led for you. Name the two or three people you would invite, and pick a week to start.
